lessons.title: Forces & Newton’s Laws
lessons.description: Forces and their properties, vector and scalar quantities, Newton's three laws of motion, and circular motion.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Force?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Forces are measured in newtons (N). Every force arises because two objects are interacting — either by touching or at a distance.

Contact forces act when objects are physically in contact. Examples include friction, normal contact force, tension, and air resistance. Non-contact forces act at a distance through fields — gravitational force, electrostatic force, and magnetic force are all non-contact forces.

Key Fact

Forces always come in pairs. When two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other. These interaction pairs can be represented as vectors.

Scalars and Vectors

A scalar quantity has magnitude only. A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Force is a vector — it has a size and acts in a particular direction. Mass is a scalar — it has only size.

Key vector quantities include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, and momentum. Key scalar quantities include distance, speed, mass, energy, and temperature.

A free body diagram shows all the forces acting on a single object. Each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the object. The length of the arrow represents the size of the force, and the direction of the arrow shows which way the force acts.

When the arrows are equal and opposite, the forces are balanced and the resultant force is zero. When they are unequal, there is a net (resultant) force and the object will accelerate.

Newton's First Law

Newton's first law states that if the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object will remain stationary or continue to move at a constant velocity in a straight line. If the resultant force is not zero, the object will accelerate — its speed or direction (or both) will change.

Key Fact

An object moving at constant velocity has a resultant force of zero. It does not need a force to keep it moving — only to change its motion.

Newton's Second Law

Newton's second law tells us that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass. The equation is:

$$F = m \times a$$

where \(F\) is the resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is the mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is the acceleration in metres per second squared (m/s²).

Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object. It is a vector quantity measured in newtons using a newton meter (spring balance). The equation is:

$$W = m \times g$$

where \(W\) is weight in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(g\) is the gravitational field strength in N/kg. On Earth, \(g \approx 9.8\) N/kg.

Mass is a scalar — it stays the same everywhere. Weight is a vector — it changes depending on the gravitational field strength.

Newton's Third Law

Newton's third law states that whenever two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These forces act on different objects, are the same type of force, and are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

For example, when you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with an equal force. When Earth pulls you downward with gravity, you pull Earth upward with the same gravitational force.

Key Fact

Newton's third law pairs are always the same type of force, act on two different objects, are equal in size, and act in opposite directions.

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. It is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration:

$$m = \frac{F}{a}$$

An object with a large inertial mass requires a large force to produce even a small acceleration. This is why it is much harder to push a loaded trolley than an empty one.

Circular Motion

An object moving in a circle at constant speed is constantly changing direction, so its velocity is changing. This means the object is accelerating, even though its speed stays the same.

For an object to move in a circle, there must be a resultant force acting towards the centre of the circle. This force is called the centripetal force. Without this force, the object would move in a straight line (Newton's first law). The centripetal force could be provided by tension, gravity, friction, or another force depending on the situation.

Exam Tip: When asked about Newton's laws, always identify the forces involved and state whether the resultant force is zero or not. For F = ma calculations, remember that F is the resultant force, not just any single force. Show your working clearly and include units in every step.

Forces are vector quantities that arise from interactions between objects. Newton's three laws explain how forces affect motion: the first law links zero resultant force to constant velocity, the second law quantifies the relationship \(F = ma\), and the third law states that forces always come in equal and opposite pairs. Understanding free body diagrams and the difference between mass and weight is essential for tackling force calculations in the exam.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:

practice_questions.text: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 2 m/s². A 900 kg car accelerates at 3 m/s². Compare the resultant forces acting on the two cars.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Car A: F = 1200 × 2 = 2400 N (1)
• Car B: F = 900 × 3 = 2700 N (1)
• Car B has a larger resultant force (1)
• Even though Car B has less mass, its greater acceleration means it needs more force / F = ma applied correctly (1)

practice_questions.text: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Explain, using Newton’s laws, how the forces on the skydiver change from the moment they jump until they reach terminal velocity.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks:
• Initially, weight acts downward and air resistance is small/zero (1)
• There is a large resultant force downward, so the skydiver accelerates (Newton’s second law) (1)
• As speed increases, air resistance increases (1)
• The resultant force decreases, so acceleration decreases (1)
• Eventually air resistance equals weight, so resultant force is zero (1)
• The skydiver moves at constant velocity (terminal velocity) — Newton’s first law (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why an astronaut weighs less on the Moon than on Earth, even though their mass stays the same.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Mass is a scalar quantity and does not change with location (1)
• Weight depends on gravitational field strength (W = mg) (1)
• The Moon has a weaker gravitational field strength than Earth, so the astronaut’s weight is less (1)

lessons.title: Momentum & Force-Time Graphs
lessons.description: Momentum calculations, conservation of momentum in collisions, Newton's second law applied to momentum, and stopping distance with safety implications.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Momentum?

Momentum is a property of any moving object. It depends on both the mass and velocity of the object. The equation for momentum is:

$$p = m \times v$$

where \(p\) is momentum in kg m/s, \(m\) is mass in kg, and \(v\) is velocity in m/s. Because velocity is a vector, momentum is also a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction.

Key Fact

Momentum = mass × velocity. A 50 kg skater moving at 4 m/s has a momentum of 200 kg m/s. Doubling the velocity doubles the momentum.

Conservation of Momentum

In a closed system (one where no external forces act), the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after it. This is the conservation of momentum.

This principle applies to all collisions and explosions. For a collision between two objects:

$$m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2'$$

In a perfectly inelastic collision, the two objects stick together and move as one after the collision. For example, a 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together:

Total momentum before = \(2 \times 3 + 1 \times 0 = 6\) kg m/s

Total momentum after = \((2 + 1) \times v = 6\), so \(v = 2\) m/s

In an explosion, the total momentum before is zero (everything is stationary). After the explosion, the momentum of each part must add to zero — the parts move in opposite directions.

Newton’s Second Law and Momentum

Newton’s second law can be written in terms of momentum. The resultant force on an object equals the rate of change of momentum:

$$F = \frac{mv - mu}{t}$$

where \(F\) is the force in newtons (N), \(mv - mu\) is the change in momentum in kg m/s, and \(t\) is the time in seconds (s). This form of the equation is particularly useful for understanding collisions and force-time graphs.

Key Fact

The area under a force-time graph equals the change in momentum (impulse). A larger force applied for a shorter time produces the same change in momentum as a smaller force applied for a longer time.

Stopping Distance

The stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance:

$$\text{stopping distance} = \text{thinking distance} + \text{braking distance}$$

Thinking distance is affected by the driver’s reaction time. Factors that increase reaction time include tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions (such as using a mobile phone), and poor visibility. A typical reaction time is 0.2–0.9 seconds.

Braking distance is affected by: the speed of the vehicle (higher speed means longer braking distance), the mass of the vehicle, the condition of the brakes, the condition of the road surface, and the amount of friction between the tyres and the road.

Increasing speed has a dramatic effect on stopping distance because both thinking distance and braking distance increase with speed. Braking distance increases with the square of the speed.

Large Decelerations and Safety

When a vehicle stops very quickly, the deceleration is very large. Using \(F = \frac{mv - mu}{t}\), if the time is very short, the force is very large. This can cause serious injuries to passengers.

Crumple zones, seat belts, and airbags all work on the same principle: they increase the time over which the momentum changes, which reduces the force experienced by the passengers. This is a direct application of the equation \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{t}\) — increasing \(t\) decreases \(F\) for the same change in momentum.

Key Fact

Safety features such as crumple zones, seat belts, and airbags increase the time of deceleration, reducing the force on passengers for the same change in momentum.

In this core practical, you vary the masses added to trolleys to investigate how force, mass, and acceleration are related. A trolley is accelerated along a track by a hanging mass. Light gates measure the acceleration.

The independent variable is the force (changed by varying the hanging mass). The dependent variable is the acceleration. The control variables include the total mass of the system. As force increases, acceleration increases proportionally (for constant mass), confirming \(F = ma\).

Exam Tip: For momentum calculations, always assign a direction as positive and stick with it. Objects moving in opposite directions have opposite signs for velocity. When using \(F = \frac{mv - mu}{t}\), remember to subtract the initial momentum from the final momentum, not the other way round.

Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity and is always conserved in a closed system. Newton’s second law links force to the rate of change of momentum, and this explains why safety features like crumple zones reduce the force in a collision by increasing the stopping time. Stopping distance depends on both thinking distance and braking distance, each affected by different factors.

practice_questions.text: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. After the collision, they stick together. Calculate the velocity after the collision and explain why kinetic energy is not conserved.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks:
• Total momentum before = 3 × 4 + 1 × 0 = 12 kg m/s (1)
• Total momentum after = (3 + 1) × v = 12 (1)
• v = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m/s (1)
• KE before = ½ × 3 × 4² = 24 J (1)
• KE after = ½ × 4 × 3² = 18 J (1)
• Some kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy / sound during the collision — it is an inelastic collision (1)

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The passengers have momentum before braking (p = mv) (1)
• Force = change in momentum ÷ time (F = Δp/t) (1)
• Because the time is very short (0.5 s), the force is very large (1)

lessons.title: Waves: Properties, Types & the Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.description: Wave properties, types, behaviour including refraction, and the electromagnetic spectrum.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Waves?

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy and information from one place to another without transferring matter. When a wave passes through water, the water molecules oscillate up and down, but the water itself does not travel with the wave — it is the wave pattern that moves.

Evidence for this comes from watching a floating object on water: it bobs up and down as waves pass, but it does not move forward with the waves. Similarly, sound waves cause air particles to vibrate back and forth, but the air itself does not travel from the source to the listener.

Key Fact

Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter. The particles of the medium oscillate about a fixed position.

Wave Properties

All waves can be described using these key terms:

Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position. Wavelength (\(\lambda\)) is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest). Frequency (\(f\)) is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Period is the time for one complete wave to pass a point.

Wave speed (\(v\)) is how fast the wave travels. A wavefront is an imaginary line joining all the points at the same phase of a wave.

Transverse and Longitudinal Waves

There are two types of wave:

In a transverse wave, the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. Examples include all electromagnetic waves, water surface waves, and waves on a string.

In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. The wave creates alternating compressions (where particles are pushed together) and rarefactions (where particles are spread apart). Sound is a longitudinal wave. Seismic P-waves are also longitudinal.

Wave speed, frequency, and wavelength are linked by the wave equation:

$$v = f \times \lambda$$

where \(v\) is wave speed in m/s, \(f\) is frequency in Hz, and \(\lambda\) is wavelength in metres (m). This equation applies to all types of wave.

Wave speed can also be calculated using:

$$v = \frac{x}{t}$$

where \(x\) is the distance travelled in metres and \(t\) is the time taken in seconds.

Key Fact

You must recall two wave equations: \(v = f \times \lambda\) and \(v = \frac{x}{t}\). Both are used in the exam and must be recalled from memory.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic (EM) spectrum is a continuous range of waves. All EM waves are transverse, transfer energy from source to observer, and travel at the same speed in a vacuum — the speed of light, approximately \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s.

The spectrum is ordered from longest wavelength (lowest frequency) to shortest wavelength (highest frequency):

Radio waves → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays

Our eyes can only detect a narrow range — the visible spectrum, which ranges from red (longest wavelength) through orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo to violet (shortest wavelength).

Radio waves: broadcasting, communications, and satellite transmissions.

Microwaves: cooking, mobile phone communications, and satellite transmissions.

Infrared: cooking, thermal imaging, short-range communications, optical fibres, TV remote controls, and security systems.

Visible light: vision, photography, and illumination.

Ultraviolet: security marking, fluorescent lamps, detecting forged banknotes, and disinfecting water.

X-rays: medical imaging, airport security scanners, and observing internal structures.

Gamma rays: sterilising food and medical equipment, detecting cancer, and cancer treatment.

The danger of electromagnetic radiation generally increases with increasing frequency. Excessive exposure can cause harm:

Microwaves: internal heating of body cells. Infrared: skin burns. Ultraviolet: damage to surface cells and eyes, potentially leading to skin cancer and eye conditions. X-rays and gamma rays: can cause mutation or damage to cells inside the body.

Refraction of Waves

When a wave crosses the boundary between two different substances, its speed changes. If the wave hits the boundary at an angle (not along the normal), this change in speed causes a change in direction — this is called refraction.

Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract, or reflect waves in ways that vary with wavelength. This is why a glass prism can split white light into the visible spectrum — different colours (wavelengths) are refracted by different amounts.

Key Fact

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (\(3 \times 10^8\) m/s), are transverse, and can be reflected, refracted, and absorbed. The danger increases with frequency.

Exam Tip: When describing the EM spectrum, state the correct order and mention that all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. For wave calculations, make sure you rearrange \(v = f \lambda\) correctly and convert units (e.g. kHz to Hz, nm to m) before substituting.

Waves transfer energy without transferring matter and come in two types: transverse (oscillations perpendicular to direction) and longitudinal (oscillations parallel to direction). The wave equation \(v = f \lambda\) links speed, frequency, and wavelength. The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous range from radio waves to gamma rays, all travelling at the speed of light in a vacuum but differing in wavelength, frequency, uses, and dangers.

lessons.title: Light, Reflection & Refraction
lessons.description: Electromagnetic waves, properties of light, reflection and refraction, interaction of waves with matter, and measuring wave speed.
lessons.content_html:
Light as an Electromagnetic Wave

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. It is part of the electromagnetic spectrum and travels at approximately \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum. Like all EM waves, light transfers energy from a source to an observer.

When light meets a surface or boundary, it can be reflected, refracted, transmitted, or absorbed. The behaviour depends on the wavelength of the light and the properties of the substance.

Key Fact

When electromagnetic waves meet a boundary between materials, they may be absorbed, transmitted, refracted, or reflected. The way they behave varies with wavelength.

Reflection

When light reflects off a smooth surface (like a plane mirror), it obeys the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal — an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray hits.

Smooth surfaces produce specular reflection, giving clear images. Rough surfaces produce diffuse reflection, scattering light in many directions.

To draw a ray diagram for reflection: (1) Draw the mirror as a straight line. (2) Draw the normal at 90° to the surface at the point where the incident ray hits. (3) Draw the incident ray arriving at the surface. (4) Measure the angle of incidence (between the incident ray and the normal). (5) Draw the reflected ray at the same angle on the other side of the normal.

Always use a ruler and protractor in the exam. Label the incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle of incidence (\(i\)), and angle of reflection (\(r\)).

Refraction

Refraction occurs when light passes from one transparent medium into another (for example, from air into glass). The light changes speed at the boundary. If it hits the boundary at an angle to the normal, it also changes direction.

When light passes from a less dense medium (like air) into a more dense medium (like glass), it slows down and bends towards the normal. When it passes from a more dense medium into a less dense medium, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

Key Fact

Light bends towards the normal when it slows down (entering a denser medium) and away from the normal when it speeds up (entering a less dense medium). A ray hitting the boundary along the normal passes straight through without bending.

In this core practical, you investigate how light refracts as it enters and exits a rectangular glass block.

Method: Place the glass block on paper and draw around it. Shine a ray of light at different angles into the block using a ray box. Mark the incident ray, the point where it enters the block, the point where it exits, and the emergent ray. Remove the block and draw the refracted ray through the block by joining the entry and exit points.

Key observations: The light bends towards the normal on entering the glass (it slows down) and bends away from the normal on leaving (it speeds up). The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways. If the angle of incidence is 0° (along the normal), no bending occurs.

The independent variable is the angle of incidence. The dependent variable is the angle of refraction. Control variables include the same glass block and the same light source.

How EM Waves Interact with Matter

Different substances absorb, transmit, refract, or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength. For example, glass transmits visible light but absorbs ultraviolet. The atmosphere transmits visible light and radio waves but absorbs most gamma rays and X-rays.

The differences in velocities of electromagnetic waves in different substances cause refraction. When EM waves pass from one material to another where they travel at a different speed, the change in speed can cause a change in direction.

Changes within atoms and their nuclei can generate electromagnetic radiation across a wide frequency range. For example, when electrons in an atom move from a higher energy level to a lower one, they emit EM radiation — the frequency depends on the energy difference.

Conversely, atoms can absorb EM radiation, causing electrons to move to higher energy levels or, at very high frequencies, causing changes within the nucleus itself. Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits, and can themselves induce oscillations in a receiving circuit.

Key Fact

In the core practical, light bends towards the normal when entering glass (slowing down) and away from the normal when leaving (speeding up). The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways.

Measuring the Speed of Waves

The speed of sound in air can be measured by timing an echo over a known distance, or by using two microphones connected to a timer. The speed of ripples on water can be measured using a ripple tank: create waves of known frequency and measure the wavelength using a strobe light or ruler, then calculate speed using \(v = f \times \lambda\).

Exam Tip: In the glass block practical, always draw the normal first, then measure angles from the normal (not from the surface). Remember that the emergent ray comes out parallel to the incident ray. If asked to explain refraction, link the change in direction to the change in speed — do not just say "light bends" without explaining why.

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave that can be reflected, refracted, transmitted, or absorbed when it meets a boundary. Reflection follows the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection). Refraction occurs because light changes speed when moving between media — it bends towards the normal when slowing down and away when speeding up. The core practical with a glass block demonstrates these principles. Different materials interact with EM radiation differently depending on wavelength, and changes in atoms can both generate and absorb electromagnetic radiation.

lessons.title: Magnetism & Electromagnets
lessons.description: Magnets, magnetic fields, electromagnets, the motor effect, and Fleming's left-hand rule.
lessons.content_html:
Magnetic Poles and Materials

Every magnet has two ends called magnetic poles. One is a north-seeking pole (north pole) and the other is a south-seeking pole (south pole). The fundamental rule of magnetism is simple: unlike poles attract and like poles repel. Two north poles push each other away, while a north and a south pole pull towards each other.

Only certain materials are magnetic. The four you need to know are iron, steel, cobalt, and nickel. These are called magnetic materials. Non-magnetic materials such as wood, plastic, copper, and aluminium are not attracted to magnets and cannot be magnetised.

Key Fact

Unlike poles attract, like poles repel. The four magnetic materials are iron, steel, cobalt, and nickel.

Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time. Bar magnets and horseshoe magnets are common examples. Once magnetised, they keep their magnetism unless heated strongly or struck repeatedly.

An induced magnet is a material that becomes magnetic only when it is placed in a magnetic field. When a piece of iron is brought close to a permanent magnet, the iron becomes an induced magnet — it is attracted to the permanent magnet. However, when the permanent magnet is removed, the iron loses most of its magnetism. This makes iron a soft magnetic material.

Steel, by contrast, is a hard magnetic material — it is more difficult to magnetise than iron, but once magnetised it keeps its magnetism. This is why permanent magnets are often made from steel or special alloys.

Permanent magnets are used in compasses, fridge magnets, loudspeakers, electric motors, and generators. They are chosen when a constant magnetic field is needed without an electricity supply.

Temporary (induced) magnets are used in electromagnets, scrapyard cranes, electric bells, and magnetic door catches. They are ideal when the magnetism needs to be switched on and off.

Magnetic Fields

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material. The field is represented using field lines. These lines always point from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet. Where the lines are close together, the field is strong. Where the lines are far apart, the field is weak.

Around a bar magnet, the field lines curve outwards from the north pole and loop back into the south pole. A uniform field has parallel, equally spaced field lines — for example, the field between two flat, opposite poles placed close together.

Key Fact

Magnetic field lines go from north to south outside the magnet. Closer lines mean a stronger field; wider spacing means a weaker field.

Plotting Compasses and the Earth’s Magnetic Field

A plotting compass is a small compass that can be placed around a magnet to map out the shape and direction of the field. The compass needle always points along the field line at that position, from north to south.

The Earth itself behaves as if it has a giant bar magnet inside it. The geographic North Pole is actually near a magnetic south pole — this is why the north-seeking end of a compass needle points towards geographic north. The fact that compass needles point north everywhere on Earth is evidence that the Earth’s core must be magnetic.

A compass needle is a small bar magnet that is free to rotate. It aligns itself with the Earth’s magnetic field. Because the Earth’s magnetic south pole is near the geographic North Pole, the north-seeking pole of the compass is attracted towards it. This behaviour — consistent at every location on the planet — is strong evidence that the Earth’s iron-nickel core is magnetic.

Electromagnetism: Current and Magnetic Fields

When an electric current flows through a conductor, it creates a magnetic field around the wire. This can be demonstrated by placing plotting compasses around a wire carrying a current — the compasses will deflect, showing circular field lines around the wire.

The magnetic field around a long straight conductor forms concentric circles centred on the wire. The direction of the field depends on the direction of the current. You can use the right-hand grip rule: point your right thumb in the direction of the current, and your fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field.

The strength of this field depends on two factors: the size of the current (a larger current produces a stronger field) and the distance from the conductor (the field is strongest close to the wire and gets weaker further away).

Key Fact

A current-carrying wire produces circular magnetic field lines around it. The field strength increases with a larger current and decreases with greater distance from the wire.

Solenoids and Electromagnets

A solenoid is a long coil of wire. When a current passes through a solenoid, each turn of the coil produces its own circular magnetic field. Inside the solenoid, these individual fields add together to create a very strong, almost uniform magnetic field along the centre. Outside the solenoid, the fields partially cancel each other out, producing a much weaker field.

The field pattern of a solenoid is very similar to that of a bar magnet — it has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. The strength of the solenoid’s magnetic field can be increased by:

  • Increasing the current flowing through the coil
  • Adding more turns of wire to the coil
  • Placing an iron core inside the solenoid

An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core. The iron core becomes an induced magnet when the current flows, greatly strengthening the field. When the current is switched off, the iron loses its magnetism almost immediately, making electromagnets very useful for applications where the magnetic field needs to be controlled — such as scrapyard cranes, electric bells, circuit breakers, and MRI scanners.

Key Fact

Inside a solenoid, the fields from individual coils add together to form a strong, nearly uniform field. Outside, they cancel to give a weaker field. Adding an iron core creates an electromagnet.

lessons.title: The Motor Effect & Electromagnetic Induction
lessons.description: Electromagnetic induction, transformers, and the National Grid's high-voltage transmission.
lessons.content_html:
The Motor Effect

When a conductor carrying an electric current is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force arises because the magnetic field around the current-carrying wire interacts with the external magnetic field from the permanent magnet. An equal and opposite force also acts on the magnet itself — this is Newton's third law in action.

The motor effect only occurs when the current and the magnetic field are not parallel. The force is greatest when the current is at right angles (perpendicular) to the magnetic field. If the current is parallel to the field, there is no force.

Key Fact

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. The direction of this force can be found using Fleming's left-hand rule.

Fleming's Left-Hand Rule

Fleming's left-hand rule allows you to work out the direction of the force (and therefore the direction the conductor moves) when the current and magnetic field directions are known. Hold your left hand so that the thumb, first finger, and second finger are all at right angles to each other:

  • Thumb = direction of the Force (motion)
  • First finger = direction of the magnetic Field (north to south)
  • Second finger = direction of the Current (conventional, positive to negative)

If either the current or the magnetic field direction is reversed, the force reverses too. If both are reversed, the force stays the same.

Calculating the Force on a Conductor

The size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field can be calculated using the equation:

$$F = B \times I \times l$$

Where \(F\) is the force in newtons (N), \(B\) is the magnetic flux density in tesla (T), \(I\) is the current in amperes (A), and \(l\) is the length of the conductor in the field in metres (m).

A wire of length 0.25 m carries a current of 4 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.3 T. Calculate the force on the wire.

\(F = B \times I \times l = 0.3 \times 4 \times 0.25 = 0.3\) N

The force on the wire is 0.3 N.

Key Fact

\(F = B \times I \times l\) — force (N) = magnetic flux density (T) × current (A) × length (m). This equation only applies when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.

How an Electric Motor Works

An electric motor uses the motor effect to produce rotation. A rectangular coil of wire is placed between the poles of a permanent magnet. When current flows through the coil, one side of the coil is pushed up and the other side is pushed down (by Fleming's left-hand rule), making the coil spin.

A split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current every half turn, ensuring that the forces on each side of the coil continue to push in the same rotational direction. Without the commutator, the coil would stop and reverse after each half turn.

Electromagnetic Induction

Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating a potential difference (and, if the circuit is complete, a current) by moving a conductor through a magnetic field, or by changing the magnetic field around a conductor. This is the principle behind generators and transformers.

The size and direction of the induced potential difference depend on several factors:

  • The speed of movement — faster movement induces a larger potential difference
  • The strength of the magnetic field — a stronger field induces a larger potential difference
  • The number of turns on the coil — more turns induce a larger potential difference
  • The direction of movement or field change — reversing the direction reverses the induced potential difference

The magnetic field produced by the induced current always opposes the original change that caused it. This is known as Lenz's law.

Transformers and the National Grid

A transformer uses electromagnetic induction to change the size of an alternating voltage. It consists of two coils of wire — a primary coil and a secondary coil — wound around a shared iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil.

A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than the primary, so the output voltage is higher than the input. A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary coil, so the output voltage is lower.

Key Fact

In the national grid, step-up transformers increase the voltage at power stations to reduce the current. Lower current means less energy is wasted as heat in the transmission cables. Step-down transformers then reduce the voltage to safe levels for homes and businesses.

For a 100% efficient transformer, the power input equals the power output. This gives the equation:

$$V_P \times I_P = V_S \times I_S$$

Where \(V_P\) and \(I_P\) are the voltage and current in the primary coil, and \(V_S\) and \(I_S\) are the voltage and current in the secondary coil. If a transformer steps up the voltage, it must step down the current by the same factor (and vice versa), so that power is conserved.

Example: A step-up transformer has a primary voltage of 230 V and a primary current of 10 A. The secondary voltage is 11,500 V. What is the secondary current?

\(V_P \times I_P = V_S \times I_S\)

\(230 \times 10 = 11{,}500 \times I_S\)

\(I_S = \frac{2300}{11500} = 0.2\) A

lessons.title: Particle Model of Matter
lessons.description: Particle model, density, changes of state, specific heat capacity, latent heat, and gas pressure.
lessons.content_html:
States of Matter and the Particle Model

All matter is made up of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are constantly moving. The particle model (also called the kinetic theory model) explains the differences between the three states of matter — solids, liquids, and gases — in terms of how the particles are arranged and how they move.

  • Solids: particles are closely packed in a regular pattern. They vibrate about fixed positions but do not move from place to place. Strong forces of attraction hold them together. This is why solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume.
  • Liquids: particles are close together but arranged randomly. They can slide past each other, which is why liquids flow and take the shape of their container. They have a fixed volume but no fixed shape.
  • Gases: particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions. The forces between them are very weak. Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume — they spread out to fill any container.
Key Fact

In solids, particles vibrate in fixed positions. In liquids, particles move past each other. In gases, particles move randomly at high speed. The strength of forces between particles decreases from solid to liquid to gas.

Density

Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume. It is calculated using the equation:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

Where \(\rho\) is density in \(\text{kg/m}^3\), \(m\) is mass in kg, and \(V\) is volume in \(\text{m}^3\).

Because particles are packed most closely in solids, solids generally have the highest density. Gases have the lowest density because their particles are spread far apart. For example, the density of iron is about \(7874 \text{ kg/m}^3\), water is \(1000 \text{ kg/m}^3\), and air is only about \(1.2 \text{ kg/m}^3\).

Regular solid: Measure the mass using a balance. Measure length, width, and height using a ruler or vernier callipers, then calculate volume (e.g. \(V = l \times w \times h\) for a cuboid). Use \(\rho = m / V\).

Irregular solid: Measure the mass on a balance. Use a displacement can (eureka can) or a measuring cylinder to find the volume by water displacement. Use \(\rho = m / V\).

Liquid: Place a measuring cylinder on a balance and zero it. Pour in the liquid, then read the mass and volume. Use \(\rho = m / V\).

Changes of State

When a substance changes state — for example, from solid to liquid (melting) or from liquid to gas (boiling) — the mass is conserved. No particles are gained or lost; only the arrangement and energy of the particles change.

The key changes of state are:

  • Melting (solid → liquid) and freezing (liquid → solid)
  • Boiling/evaporation (liquid → gas) and condensation (gas → liquid)
  • Sublimation (solid → gas directly, without passing through the liquid state)

These are physical changes — unlike chemical changes, the original substance can be recovered if the change is reversed. The particles themselves do not change; only their spacing and movement alter.

Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity, and Latent Heat

When you heat a substance, the energy stored inside it increases. This is called internal energy. If the substance is not changing state, the added energy raises its temperature — the particles move faster. If the substance is changing state (e.g. melting or boiling), the temperature stays constant while the energy is used to break bonds between particles.

Specific heat capacity (\(c\)) tells you how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C. The equation is:

$$\Delta Q = m \times c \times \Delta \theta$$

Where \(\Delta Q\) is the change in thermal energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(c\) is specific heat capacity (J/kg °C), and \(\Delta \theta\) is the change in temperature (°C).

Key Fact

Specific latent heat (\(L\)) is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without any change in temperature. The equation is: \(Q = m \times L\).

Place a known mass of water in an insulated beaker. Use an immersion heater connected to a joulemeter to heat the water. Record the temperature rise using a thermometer. Calculate \(c\) using \(c = \frac{\Delta Q}{m \times \Delta \theta}\). The accepted value for water is \(4200 \text{ J/kg} \degree\text{C}\). Results may differ due to energy lost to the surroundings.

Reducing Unwanted Energy Transfer

Thermal insulation reduces unwanted energy transfers from buildings and objects. Methods include using materials with low thermal conductivity (such as foam, fibreglass, or trapped air), double glazing (a layer of air or vacuum between two panes of glass reduces conduction and convection), cavity wall insulation, loft insulation, and reflective surfaces to reduce radiation.

Gas Pressure and Temperature

Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container. The more frequent and forceful these collisions, the higher the pressure. When the temperature of a gas increases, its particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. If the volume is kept constant, the faster-moving particles hit the walls more frequently and with greater force, so the pressure increases.

Absolute zero is the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy and effectively stop moving. It is −273 °C, which equals 0 kelvin (0 K). To convert between Celsius and kelvin, use:

$$\text{temperature in K} = \text{temperature in} \degree\text{C} + 273$$

Key Fact

Absolute zero is −273 °C (0 K). At this temperature, particles have minimum kinetic energy. To convert: K = °C + 273.

lessons.title: Forces & Matter
lessons.description: Hooke's law, spring constant, elastic potential energy, and force-extension graphs.
lessons.content_html:
Stretching, Bending, and Compressing

When forces act on an object, they can change its shape. An object can be stretched, bent, or compressed. In every case, more than one force is required to change the shape — a single force would simply cause the object to accelerate rather than deform. For example, to stretch a spring you must pull both ends in opposite directions, or fix one end and pull the other.

Key Fact

Stretching, bending, or compressing an object always requires more than one force. A single force would cause acceleration, not deformation.

Elastic and Inelastic Distortion

When a force deforms an object, the deformation can be either elastic distortion or inelastic distortion.

In elastic distortion, the object returns to its original shape and size once the force is removed. A stretched rubber band that springs back to its original length is an example of elastic behaviour. In inelastic distortion, the object is permanently deformed — it does not return to its original shape. Bending a paperclip is an example of inelastic distortion.

A spring behaves elastically as long as it is not stretched beyond its elastic limit. Beyond this point, the spring undergoes inelastic distortion and will not return to its original length when the force is removed.

Hooke’s Law

Hooke’s law states that the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the elastic limit is not exceeded. The equation is:

$$F = k \times x$$

Where \(F\) is the force applied in newtons (N), \(k\) is the spring constant in newtons per metre (N/m), and \(x\) is the extension in metres (m).

A stiffer spring has a larger spring constant — it requires more force to produce the same extension. The spring constant can be found by rearranging the equation: \(k = \frac{F}{x}\).

A spring has a spring constant of 40 N/m. Calculate the force needed to extend the spring by 0.15 m.

\(F = k \times x = 40 \times 0.15 = 6\) N

The force needed is 6 N.

Key Fact

Hooke’s law: \(F = k \times x\). The extension is directly proportional to the force, but only up to the elastic limit. Beyond this point, the relationship is no longer linear and the spring does not return to its original length.

Force-Extension Graphs

A force-extension graph shows the relationship between force and extension for a material. For a spring obeying Hooke’s law, the graph is a straight line through the origin — this is a linear relationship. The gradient of the straight-line section equals the spring constant \(k\).

If the spring is stretched beyond its elastic limit, the graph curves — the extension increases more quickly for each additional unit of force. This is a non-linear relationship. The point where the line starts to curve marks the elastic limit.

Different materials produce different shaped graphs. A rubber band, for example, does not obey Hooke’s law — its force-extension graph is curved from the start. It still returns to its original shape (elastic), but the relationship between force and extension is non-linear.

Energy Stored in a Stretched Spring

When a spring is stretched (or compressed) within its elastic limit, work is done on the spring, and energy is stored as elastic potential energy. The amount of energy stored can be calculated using the equation:

$$E = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times x^2$$

Where \(E\) is the energy transferred in stretching (joules, J), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(x\) is the extension (m). This equation only applies when the spring obeys Hooke’s law — within the elastic limit.

A spring with a spring constant of 80 N/m is stretched by 0.10 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.

\(E = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times x^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.10^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 0.01 = 0.4\) J

The elastic potential energy stored is 0.4 J.

Key Fact

Elastic potential energy: \(E = \frac{1}{2} k x^2\). This equation applies only when the spring obeys Hooke’s law (within the elastic limit). Notice that energy depends on extension squared — doubling the extension quadruples the energy stored.

Core Practical: Investigating Springs

In this required practical, you investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring and calculate the work done.

  • Method: Clamp a spring vertically. Measure its natural (unstretched) length with a ruler. Add masses one at a time, recording the new length each time. Calculate the extension (new length minus original length) for each mass.
  • Variables: Independent variable = force (weight of masses). Dependent variable = extension. Control variables = same spring, same starting position, same measuring equipment.
  • Analysis: Plot a force-extension graph. The straight-line region confirms Hooke’s law. The gradient equals the spring constant. If the line curves, the elastic limit has been exceeded.
  • Accuracy: Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax error. Wait for the spring to stop oscillating before reading. Repeat readings and calculate a mean to improve reliability.
